transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE); Jordan Patel (Redwood SE); Nina Ortiz (CSM); Marta López (Copperfield Head of ML); Samir Rao (CTO); Emily Park (Platform Engineer); Jonah McKee (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Quick economic intake to map Copperfield's throughput/budget to hosting options. Key asks: visible per-token math, examples of batching gains, how prefix caching helps order-history prompts, and what dedicated reserved commitments reduce.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood): All right hi everyone thanks for joining, um we can kick off. I'm Alex, I'm the AE for your account, joined by Jordan our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Marta (Copperfield): Doing good, thanks. Sorry for the slight delay, timezone juggling.
[00:12] Samir (Copperfield): All good. We have about 50 minutes — want to make sure we get cost mapping and next steps.
[00:20] Alex: Perfect. We'll, um, aim for intro then go deep on unit economics then tradeoffs. Jordan will show some rough numbers.
[00:27] Jordan (Redwood): Quick context — Copperfield mentioned wanting to power order-tracking and SLA-sensitive routing responses. You're looking at ~200 qps peak for read-type prompts with average 400 tokens per request, and some longer exception flows up to 2k tokens. Is that still accurate?
[00:40] Emily (Copperfield): Yeah 200 qps is a top-end spike during morning batch windows; typical steady state is 50-70 qps. The average 400 excludes the history chunk we attach — with history it's closer to 660 tokens.
[00:52] Alex: Great, so there are two dimensions to optimize: reduce per-token cost via batching/caching and pick hosting mode that aligns with burst profile.
[01:05] Jordan: I'll start with a simplified per-token example — hosted baseline: our public API rate priced as $0.0008 per input token / $0.0016 per output token for this model-family (example numbers). If you do naive no-batching calls at 200 qps and 400 tokens output on average, that scales quickly. But continuous batching reduces the effective per-token compute by improving GPU utilization.
[01:32] Marta: Sorry can you expand on batching? We saw numbers in the deck but not sure how it maps to our latency needs.
[01:40] Jordan: Totally. So batching groups concurrent requests into a single GPU forward pass when latency SLO permits. If you have a 50 ms SLO headroom, we can batch much more aggressively than a 10 ms SLO. Two levers: max batch window (ms) and batch size cap. In practice for 200 qps and 50–100 ms window we often hit 8–16x effective token reduction on per-request overhead, not token compute, so cost drops ~20–50% depending on sequence length distribution.
[02:08] Emily: That 50–100 ms window would be acceptable for our non-realtime tracking. The customer-facing SLA is 200–300 ms P95 though.
[02:16] Jordan: Right, so we need to design the request routing so that critical paths bypass batching (or use smaller batch windows) and bulk non-critical paths get full batching. That's where routing policies come in.
[02:28] Samir: How about prefix caching — we append user order-history; can that be cached?
[02:33] Jordan: Yes, prefix/KV cache is very helpful. If you have a consistent order-history chunk, we can cache first N tokens' KV and only run the new portion. For many of our customers that's a 30–60% token compute reduction on repeat queries. But it depends on hit rate — if users have very dynamic history then hit rate drops.
[02:53] Marta: Our hit rate should be decent; many users only ask about recent orders. Question — does caching change data residency rules? We need to keep PII within our VPC.
[03:03] Alex: Good note — for Private/Dedicated we support customer-managed networking and KMS for keys. Cache objects in Redwood Dedicated can be stored in the customer's VPC when using Private deployment; for Hosted we encrypt and retain per our standard retention policies, but we can discuss custom retention in enterprise contracts.
[03:22] Jonah (Product): On the economics side — what are concrete numbers we can expect after batching and caching? If we assume 60% cache hit and batching yields 30% cost reduction what's the net?
[03:33] Jordan: Ballpark math: naive per-request token compute = input+output; with base hosted price let's say 1.6x10^-3 per output token. If average total tokens per request 660, naive cost ~ $1.06 per 1000 requests? (note: numbers approximate). With 30% batching savings and 60% cache hit that reduces effective compute maybe by ~55% so roughly half the naive cost. We'll send exact sheets.
[03:58] Marta: We need examples for hosted vs dedicated reserved: how much do we save if we commit to reserved capacity?
[04:05] Jordan: Reserved capacity (Dedicated) gives you lower per-token compute because you amortize GPUs across committed throughput. Roughly speaking, a small dedicated pool with reserved commitment can cut unit compute cost 20–40% relative to hosted list price for sustained workloads. There's a break-even point: short-lived spikes usually favor hosted; sustained high QPS favors dedicated.
[04:26] Samir: What about burst capacity — we have those morning spikes. Can dedicated automatically burst into hosted?
[04:32] Alex: Yes, hybrid routing: primary Dedicated pool then overflow to Hosted fallbacks. We can set policies to prefer cheaper variants or smaller quantized models when fallback happens. That gives you predictable base cost but still handles spikes.
[04:45] Emily: If we fallback to a quantized model variant, how different is output quality? For order-tracking it's likely fine but exceptions (refund semantics) are sensitive.
[04:54] Jordan: Quantized variants are usually good for many tasks; but we recommend running quality evals on your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization points and flag regressions. Typical degraded cases show minor syntactic oddities but often preserve intent.
[05:12] Marta: Regarding compliance — SOC2 is a must, and we need SAML SSO and RBAC. Also audit logs retained 1 year.
[05:21] Nina (Redwood CSM): We have SOC2 Type II docs, SSO/SAML integrations, RBAC, and enterprise audit log packages. We'll include the package and retention options.
[05:29] Samir: Network-wise we prefer VPC peering for Private so tokens and logs never leave our network.
[05:35] Alex: Noted. For Private we provide a customer-managed control plane and KMS options. For Dedicated we can offer VPC peering and restricted egress.
[05:44] Jonah: Back to cost math, can you run a sensitivity with two axes: token avg (400 vs 660) and cache hit (0%, 40%, 60%)?
[05:53] Jordan: Yep Jordan: that's exactly what we'll simulate in the spreadsheet; we can show cost per 1M requests and show break-even lines for dedicated thresholds.
[06:02] Marta: Is there a quick rule of thumb: at what sustained qps should we go Dedicated?
[06:07] Jordan: Rule-of-thumb depends on tokens/throughput but rough threshold for our current model family is sustained ~80–120 qps (with 400–600 tokens) to consider small dedicated. But again it depends on commit term — 12 month reserved commitment gets better rates.
[06:21] Samir: We have about 3-month runway to decide procurement. Would like an internal pilot before committing.
[06:27] Alex: Makes sense. We typically do a 1–2 week pilot where we run your prompts against hosted and a dedicated-like configuration on our side to measure latency and cost. Jordan will propose the scope.
[06:37] Emily: For pilot data, do you need actual PII or can we synthetic? We prefer synthetic but realistic distributions.
[06:43] Jordan: Synthetic is fine for perf; for quality evals you may want a sanitized sample. For cache effectiveness we'll need similar token distributions.
[06:53] Marta: Slight tangent — you mentioned model variants earlier. Can Redwood route between model families based on cost tiers automatically?
[06:59] Jordan: Yes policy-based routing — criteria like latency, cost-per-token threshold, or health. You can define fallbacks: e.g., if P95 latency > 400ms route to small-quant model or to hosted cheaper pool.
[07:12] Samir: Any mention of egress costs or hidden fees? We prefer transparent unit costs.
[07:17] Alex: We pride on transparency — our invoices show token-level breakdown and per-route cost. For Private deployments some infra egress costs are passed through but we document them up front.
[07:26] Jonah: Is there any licensing or minimum for the private deployment?
[07:30] Alex: Private has a platform fee and usually an initial onboarding professional services engagement; specifics depend on scope and region. We'll include ballpark numbers in the doc.
[07:39] Marta: Ok let's go through a quick worked example — Jordan can you do a back-of-envelope for 1M requests per day at avg 660 tokens and 60% cache hit?
[07:47] Jordan: Sure. 1M requests * 660 tokens = 660M tokens raw. With 60% cache hit we only compute 40% of that tokens = 264M effective tokens. With batching assume 30% less cost so ~185M effective token-equivalents. If baseline hosted cost per token is 0.0008 USD (example) then monthly cost ~ $148k. Dedicated could reduce that by 30% so ~$104k. These are illustrative — we'll put precise numbers in the spreadsheet with your true model choices.
[08:22] Samir: These are useful. I also want to call out multi-region latency — some of our users are in EU and APAC. Does Redwood support regional model endpoints?
[08:31] Alex: Yes, Hosted has multiple regions; Dedicated pools can be regionally deployed too for lower latency. For Private we can deploy on prem or in specific cloud regions.
[08:40] Jonah: Any non-obvious levers teams forget?
[08:43] Jordan: Two big ones: tokenization hygiene (sometimes prompts include redundant whitespace or repeated IDs that inflate token counts) and prompt templating to maximize cache hits. Also using structured outputs to reduce output tokens.
[08:57] Emily: Nice — we'll do a token audit.
[09:00] Marta: For the pilot, what success criteria do you recommend? Cost per 1k requests below X, P95 latency under Y, and quality pass-rate above <z>?
[09:09] Jordan: Exactly. We usually recommend: P95 under 300ms for critical flows, cost per 1k requests under target you set, and quality evals on curated prompt bundle with acceptable edit distance / semantic score thresholds.
[09:21] Alex: Let's plan to define those targets in the next week and then run pilot measurements.

[09:30] -- mid-call technical detour --
[09:31] Jordan: (screenshare) I'll show a quick throughput table — apologies, audio might be poor for a sec.
[09:42] Speaker 1: (murmur)
[09:50] Jordan: Okay, so this table shows dedicated small pool (2xA100 equiv) hitting sustained 120 qps at 400 tokens with p95 180ms; at 200 qps you need 4x equivalent. Batching curves taper at longer sequences.
[10:12] Marta: How do you model concurrency on our side vs request queuing? We can't have unbounded latency.
[10:18] Jordan: We expose both queue-length and latency SLO metrics. You can drop to async patterns for non-critical requests or implement client-side rate-limiters.
[10:26] Samir: Any vendor lock concerns when moving from hosted to private?
[10:30] Alex: We aim for portability — models are standard checkpoints and we provide export options for model artifacts where permitted by license. The orchestration layer is our IP so migrating operational policies requires some work but not impossible.
[10:41] Jonah: What about pricing cadence: do hosted prices change often? We want predictability.
[10:46] Alex: Hosted list price is stable, but we offer committed discounts for reserved capacity and volume tiers in contracts. We'll propose a pricing ladder for you.
[10:52] Samir: Ok. On procurement — what compliance docs do you need from us to start a pilot?
[10:58] Nina: For pilots we usually need an NDA and basic IP/data handling questionnaire. For dedicated or private we add more security paperwork.
[11:05] Marta: We'll get those to you.

[11:12] -- near end recap --
[11:13] Alex: Quick recap: 1) Jordan will run the cost sensitivity spreadsheets (token avg vs cache hit); 2) Alex will email unit-econ sheet and initial hosting scenarios; 3) Customer to provide sample prompts and target SLOs; 4) schedule a 1-week pilot window to run hosted + dedicated-like runs; 5) Redwood to include SOC2 and network docs. Any additions?
[11:33] Samir: Please include example invoice lines so finance can forecast.
[11:37] Alex: Will do.
[11:39] Jonah: Also include recommended routing policy example to handle morning spikes.
[11:43] Jordan: I'll include a suggested policy snippet and a rough guardrail config.
[11:47] Marta: Thanks all. This is helpful.
[11:50] Alex: Great — we'll follow up with the materials by Monday.
[11:53] Samir: Thanks everyone.
[11:55] Meeting ended.

Post-call notes (auto): Pilot scope agreed; spreadsheet and security docs promised. Action owners captured above.
